'''Heather Cecile Allen''' is a research chemist and Professor of Chemistry, who leads the Allen Group at The [[Ohio State University]]. Allen's research focuses on [[Interface (chemistry)|interfacial phenomena]], particularly those involving water and air. Her work has broad application ranging from medicine to climate change. She also develops nonlinear optical spectroscopy and microscopy instruments for the examination of interfacial surfaces <ref name="GoogleScholar">{{Cite web|title=Heather C. Allen – Google Scholar Profile|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=xtke6AcAAAAJ|website=Google Scholar|access-date=2025-09-01}}</ref><ref name=OSUCV2014>{{cite web|title=Heather Cecile == Education ==
Heather Allen enrolled at [[Saddleback College]], a community college, as an adult student at age 28.  Interested in [[environmental science]], she won a Science Scholarship Foundation Fellowship, enabling her to transfer to the [[University of California, Irvine]] to earn a chemistry or chemical engineering degree.<ref name=Wilkinson>{{cite journal|last1=Wilkinson|first1=Sophie L.|title=Starting from scratch: new professors share their experiences|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=June 19, 2000|volume=78|issue=25|pages=41–47|url=http://pubs.acs.org/cen/coverstory/7825/7825scit1.html|accessdate=December 16, 2015|doi=10.1021/cen-v078n025.p041|url-access=subscription}}</ref> She received her B.S. degree in chemistry from the University of California, Irvine in 1993, working as a research assistant with Nobel Laureate [[Frank Sherwood Rowland]] and [[Donald R. Blake]].  She received her Ph.D. in [[physical chemistry]] in 1997, working with  [[John C. Hemminger]] and [[Barbara J. Finlayson-Pitts]]. The topic of her Ph.D. thesis was ''Fundamental surface processes in heterogeneous atmospheric chemistry: Applications to sea-salt (NaCl) and oxide particulate chemistry.''<ref name=ADD1996>{{cite book|title=American doctoral dissertations, 1996–1997.|date=1998|oclc= 795384415|page=153|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7jzgAAAAMAAJ&q=Heather+Cecile+Allen+%22University+of+California+Irvine%22}}</ref> She received several awards and postdoctoral fellowships, and did postdoctoral work with [[Geraldine L. Richmond]] at the [[University of Oregon]].<ref name=Tree>{{cite web|title=Heather C. Allen|url=http://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=69301|website=Chemistry Tree|accessdate=December 16, 2015}}</ref>

== Career ==
Heather Allen joined [[Ohio State University]] in 2000, as an assistant professor of environmental chemistry.<ref name=Wilkinson/> She went on to become a full professor in the department of chemistry and biochemistry and in the department of pathology. She leads the Allen Group at Ohio State University.<ref name=OhioStateCV>{{cite web|title=Heather Allen|url=http://chemistry.osu.edu/faculty/allen|website=The Ohio State University|accessdate=December 16, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151110173547/http://chemistry.osu.edu/faculty/allen|archive-date=November 10, 2015|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=AllenGroup>{{cite web|title=Allen Group|url=http://web.chemistry.ohio-state.edu/~allen/|website=The Ohio State University|accessdate=December 16, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110817102239/http://web.chemistry.ohio-state.edu/~allen/|archive-date=August 17, 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Interfacial phenomena===
Her research focuses on fundamental [[Interface (chemistry)|interfacial phenomena]], the molecular organization and orientation at interfaces between [[gases]] and [[liquids]], gases and [[solids]], and liquids and solids.<ref name=OhioStateCV/> She is particularly interested in understanding the activities of [[ions]] and [[molecules]] in aqueous surface structures. Understanding molecular organization is essential to understanding the ways in which surfaces will react.<ref name=scholar/> Her studies of chemical reaction mechanisms have examined [[water]], [[lipids]], and [[fatty acids]], among others.<ref name=OhioStateCV/><ref name=rainbow>{{cite book|last1=Ho|first1=Mae-Wan|title=Living rainbow H₂O|date=2012|publisher=World Scientific|location=Singapore|isbn=978-9814390897|pages=161–166|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=M1bR3LLnv5kC&q=%22Heather+C.+Allen%22}}</ref>

Her work has relevance to a wide variety of fields, from [[medicine]] to [[climate change]]. Medically, aqueous surface structures are particularly relevant in the understanding of cell membranes and skin surfaces, which function as gateways to the cell and the body.  As a [[Beckman Young Investigators Award|Beckman Young Investigator]], Allen studied the biophysics of the [[lung]] as a barrier mediating [[oxygen]] and [[carbon dioxide]] transport, and the importance of [[pulmonary surfactants]].<ref name=NovelDiscoveries/> Air, lipids, and water are all involved at the surface of the lung.  Molecules of the alveolar lining were found to be important in the efficiency with which the lung could function.<ref name=Columbus>{{cite web|title=Columbus Events Sept 18 – 25|url=http://taniaexplorescolumbus.com/2013/09/24/1187/|website=Tania explores Columbus|date=September 24, 2013|accessdate=December 18, 2015}}</ref>

Allen has also examined the development of [[Biological membrane|biomembranes]] with particular application to the detection of [[cancer]] margins.<ref name=NovelDiscoveries/> Her team is working on the development of infrared [[Biomarker (medicine)|biomarkers]] and molecular level diagnostics for the use of cancer surgeons.<ref name=Chen>{{cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Zhaomin|last2=Butke|first2=Ryan|last3=Miller|first3=Barrie|last4=Hitchcock|first4=Charles L.|last5=Allen|first5=Heather C.|last6=Povoski|first6=Stephen P.|last7=Martin|first7=Edward W.|last8=Coe|first8=James V.|title=Infrared Metrics for Fixation-Free Liver Tumor Detection|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry B|date=October 17, 2013|volume=117|issue=41|pages=12442–12450|doi=10.1021/jp4073087|pmc=3875153|pmid=24053455}}</ref>

Allen's studies of interfacial phenomena are also relevant to [[geophysics]], [[geochemistry]] and [[climate]]. Her work includes studies of how ions and minerals interact at surfaces where they are involved in [[corrosion]] and the interactions of [[pollutants]] with [[soil]].<ref name=Wilkinson/>

The effect of particles at surfaces is important in understanding the behavior of air and water at ocean surfaces, and the health of oceans.  Recent research indicates that accumulated ions are present in the ocean's surface layers. Using highly accurate laser beams, researchers were able to see the structures formed by halogen ions, or [[halides]], and surrounding molecules of water in the interfacial area. Halides such as [[iodide]] and [[bromide]] were found close to the surface,<ref name=Wagner/> a result which challenged "conventional wisdom" on the subject.<ref name=NSF2004/> [[Chloride]] ions were found lower down.<ref name=Wagner/><ref name=NSF2004/> Iodide and bromide are unstable and tend to combine with other chemicals to form ozone.<ref name=Wagner/> This means that fog and ocean spray are more chemically reactive than was previously believed by scientists. Allen's results may cause atmospheric chemists to revise their models of ozone activity and climate change.<ref name=Wagner/><ref name=NSF2004/>

The behavior of atmospheric aerosols, particulate matter suspended in the atmosphere, is also related to climate change.<ref name=NASA>{{cite web|last1=Allen|first1=Bob|title=Atmospheric Aerosols: What Are They, and Why Are They So Important?|url=http://www.nasa.gov/centers/langley/news/factsheets/Aerosols.html|website=NASA|date=July 31, 2015}}</ref> Heather Allen is part of a national multidisciplinary group of researchers involved in the [[Center for Aerosol Impacts on Climate and the Environment]] (CAICE) who study the effects of atmospheric aerosols.<ref name=CAICE>{{cite web|title=Ohio State Chemist's Work to Benefit From $20 Million NSF CAICE Grant|url=http://artsandsciences.osu.edu/news/ohio-state-chemists-work-to-benefit-from-20-million-nsf-caice-grant|website=Ohio State University|date=September 16, 2013}}</ref>  Allen studies the surfaces of cloud systems and their electric fields, to better understand thunderstorms, lightning strikes and the effects of microdroplets on clouds and fogs.  With Lisa Van Loon, she has examined the behavior of [[sulfuric acid]] and [[methanol]], found as aerosols in the upper atmosphere.  Together they can form [[methyl sulfate]], a compound that attracts water droplets and supports cloud formation. While sulfuric acid can reflect light and heat, clouds tend to trap light and heat in the atmosphere. The interplay between sulfuric acid and atmospheric temperature change is therefore more complex than originally thought.<ref name=Loon>{{cite news|last1=Wagner|first1=Holly|title=Atmospheric compound is double-edged sword in climate change |url=http://researchnews.osu.edu/archive/sulmeth.htm|accessdate=December 18, 2015|work=Ohio State Research|date=December 8, 2003}}</ref>

{{blockquote|“Aerosols are a major driver of climate change and have major impacts... their effect depends on their composition, size, surface properties, where they’re located in the environment—especially their inherent ability to scatter light, and clouds—all are variables.” Heather C. Allen<ref name=CAICE/>}}

===Instrumentation===
Heather Allen and the Allen Group are involved in the design of nonlinear optical [[spectroscopy]] and [[microscopy]] instruments for scientific research. These include [[VSFG | vibrational sum frequency generation (VSFG) spectroscopy]],<ref name=Jubb>{{cite journal|last1=Jubb|first1=Aaron M.|last2=Hua|first2=Wei|last3=Allen|first3=Heather C.|title=Environmental Chemistry at Vapor/Water Interfaces: Insights from Vibrational Sum Frequency Generation Spectroscopy|journal=Annual Review of Physical Chemistry|date=May 5, 2012|volume=63|issue=1|pages=107–130|doi=10.1146/annurev-physchem-032511-143811|pmid=22224702|bibcode=2012ARPC...63..107J|s2cid=46142455}}</ref><ref name=Ma>{{cite journal|last1=Ma|first1=G|last2=Allen|first2=HC|title=New insights into lung surfactant monolayers using vibrational sum frequency generation spectroscopy.|journal=Photochemistry and Photobiology|date=2006|volume=82|issue=6|pages=1517–29|pmid=16930094|doi=10.1562/2006-06-30-IR-958|s2cid=43903916}}</ref> and broad-bandwidth sum frequency generation (BBSFG) spectroscopy, used for investigating gas-liquid and solid interfaces.<ref name=Hommel>{{cite journal|last1=Hommel|first1=EL|last2=Ma|first2=G|last3=Allen|first3=HC|title=Broadband vibrational sum frequency generation spectroscopy of a liquid surface|journal=Analytical Sciences|date=November 2001|volume=17|issue=11|pages=1325–9|pmid=11759518|doi=10.2116/analsci.17.1325|s2cid=22500496 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=DPPC>{{cite journal|last1=Ma|first1=Gang|last2=Allen|first2=Heather C.|title=DPPC Langmuir Monolayer at the Air−Water Interface: Probing the Tail and Head Groups by Vibrational Sum Frequency Generation Spectroscopy|journal=Langmuir|date=June 2006|volume=22|issue=12|pages=5341–5349|doi=10.1021/la0535227|pmid=16732662|s2cid=12630121}}<!--|accessdate=December 18, 2015--></ref>  Laser technology uses ultra-fast [[femtosecond]] and [[picosecond]] laser pulses to examine molecular-level interfaces and observe the orientation and structure of the chemical species within the surface regime, the surface signature.<ref name=femtosecond>{{cite journal|last1=Hommel|first1=EL|last2=Allen|first2=HC|title=Broadband sum frequency generation with two regenerative amplifiers: temporal overlap of femtosecond and picosecond light pulses.|journal=Analytical Sciences|date=January 2001|volume=17|issue=1|pages=137–9|pmid=11993650|doi=10.2116/analsci.17.137|s2cid=41658795 |doi-access=free}}</ref> Other techniques used and studied include polarized [[Raman spectroscopy|Raman]] and [[infrared spectroscopy]] techniques, [[Brewster angle microscope|Brewster angle microscopy]], and [[differential optical absorption spectroscopy]].<ref name=benzene>{{cite journal|last1=Hommel|first1=EL|last2=Allen|first2=HC|title=The air-liquid interface of benzene, toluene, m-xylene, and mesitylene: a sum frequency, Raman, and infrared spectroscopic study.|journal=The Analyst|date=June 2003|volume=128|issue=6|pages=750–5|pmid=12866899|doi=10.1039/b301032p|bibcode=2003Ana...128..750H|s2cid=9410214}}</ref><ref name=Brewster>{{cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Xiangke|last2=Huang|first2=Zishuai|last3=Hua|first3=Wei|last4=Castada|first4=Hardy|last5=Allen|first5=Heather C.|title=Reorganization and Caging of DPPC, DPPE, DPPG, and DPPS Monolayers Caused by Dimethylsulfoxide Observed Using Brewster Angle Microscopy|journal=Langmuir|date=December 21, 2010|volume=26|issue=24|pages=18902–18908|doi=10.1021/la102842a|pmid=21086993|s2cid=207720748}}</ref><ref name=Beekman>{{cite thesis|last1=Beekman|first1=Christopher Paul|title=Differential Optical Absorption Spectroscopy of Trace Gas Species and Aerosols in the Upper Ohio River Valley (Ph.D. thesis)|date=2010|publisher=Ohio State University|url=http://rave.ohiolink.edu/etdc/view?acc_num=osu1268143515}}</ref>
